transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

I'm here because I just can't stop worrying about how awful my face looks. The shape of my nose is completely crooked, and I have these horrible scars and acne all over my skin that have totally ruined my appearance. It's so noticeable, and I feel so ugly.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time checking your face in the mirror, trying to hide these areas, or comparing your appearance to others?

Yes, I'm constantly checking my reflection in every mirror or window I pass, and I spend hours trying to camouflage my skin with heavy makeup and styling my hair to cover my face. I also can't stop comparing my complexion to people I see in public or online, because it feels like everyone else has absolutely perfect skin.
How certain are you that these flaws are as noticeable to other people as they are to you? Do you feel absolutely convinced that others are judging or mocking you because of them?

I'm not entirely sure if people are actually mocking me, but I feel incredibly self-conscious whenever I'm around others. I constantly worry that they will notice my flaws and judge me for them. It just feels so real to me, even if I can't be certain of what they are thinking.

latest_inference.note: Previously, the candidates were ['Body Dysmorphic Disorder', 'Delusional Disorder', 'Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder']. Delusional Disorder is ruled out because the patient exhibits insight regarding their appearance concerns ('I'm not entirely sure if people are actually mocking me... I can't be certain'). Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder is ruled out as the repetitive behaviors and preoccupations are exclusively focused on physical appearance, which is better characterized by Body Dysmorphic Disorder. Therefore, the sole diagnosis is Body Dysmorphic Disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a severe preoccupation with perceived defects in their physical appearance (nose shape, facial scars, and acne) that are not prominent to others. This preoccupation leads to significant distress and repetitive behaviors, including excessive mirror-checking, intensive camouflaging (makeup and hair styling), and constant comparison with others, meeting the criteria for Body Dysmorphic Disorder.
